# Dysphagia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the esophagus > Dysphagia*

[Original Article Link](/library/Er08Qh)

---

## Summary

Dysphagia is a nonspecific symptom that refers to difficulty in <u>swallowing</u>. When present, it should be considered a <u>red flag</u> feature for a potentially serious underlying condition and should be evaluated thoroughly. <u>Oropharyngeal dysphagia</u> refers to difficulty in initiating the <u>swallowing</u> process and is typically associated with <u>coughing</u> or choking. <u>Esophageal dysphagia</u> refers to the impaired passage of a food bolus from the <u>esophagus</u> to the <u>stomach</u>. Dysphagia predominantly with <u>solid foods</u> is usually caused by a mechanical obstruction (e.g., <u>esophageal stricture</u>, oropharyngeal <u>abscess</u>). Dysphagia with liquids and solid food typically indicates a neuromuscular disorder (e.g., <u>esophageal motility disorders</u>, <u>neurodegenerative conditions</u>). Acute dysphagia is commonly caused by <u>food bolus impaction</u> or <u>stroke</u>. Depending on the suspected etiology, the diagnostic workup can include an endoscopic evaluation of the <u>nasopharynx</u> and/or <u>esophagus</u>, a <u>barium swallow</u>, and <u>high-resolution manometry</u>. <u>Neuroimaging</u> and <u>laboratory studies</u> should also be considered as needed. Supportive therapy (e.g., <u>swallowing</u> <u>rehabilitation</u>, measures to minimize <u>aspiration</u> risk) is the mainstay of management, especially in patients with <u>oropharyngeal dysphagia</u>; etiology-specific management (e.g., esophageal dilation, antimicrobials for <u>infectious esophagitis</u>) may be feasible in some conditions. In elderly patients with dysphagia, <u>goals of care</u> should be discussed before considering interventional management.

---

## Definitions

* Dysphagia: any difficulty <u>swallowing</u>, which can be divided into the following subtypes

* Oropharyngeal dysphagia: difficulty initiating the <u>swallowing</u> process

* Esophageal dysphagia: the impaired passage of solid food and liquid through the <u>esophagus</u> towards the <u>stomach</u>

* Motility-related dysphagia: dysphagia due to a neurological or muscular defect

* Structural dysphagia: dysphagia due to a mechanical or anatomical obstruction

* Aphagia: the inability to swallow

* Presbyphagia: the characteristic changes and mild decline in <u>swallowing</u> function seen in older adults; typically asymptomatic [[2]](/library/8TcOsb0)

* <u>Odynophagia</u>: a painful sensation triggered by <u>swallowing</u>





References: [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[4]](/library/t1bXis)

---

## Etiology

The following table provides an overview of the etiologies of nonacute dysphagia. <u>Food bolus impaction</u> is a common cause of acute dysphagia but is often triggered by an underlying esophageal etiology.




| <br>Overview of causes of dysphagia [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[5]](/library/kIYm1q)[[6]](/library/8bbOvH)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Motility-related dysphagia</u> | <u>Structural dysphagia</u> |
| <u>Oropharyngeal dysphagia</u> | <br><br>* Neurological disorders<br><br>* <u>Stroke</u><br><br>* <u>Neurodegenerative diseases</u><br><br>* <u>Parkinson disease</u><br><br>* <u>Brain tumor</u><br><br>* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u><br><br>* <u>Cerebral palsy</u><br><br>* <u>Guillain-Barré syndrome</u><br><br>* Other (e.g., <u>iatrogenic</u> nerve damage, <u>post-polio syndrome</u>)<br><br>* Muscular disorders<br><br>* <u>Myasthenia gravis</u><br><br>* <u>Progressive muscular dystrophies</u><br><br>* <u>Paraneoplastic syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Sarcoidosis</u><br><br>* Mixed <u>connective tissue disorders</u> (e.g., <u>systemic sclerosis</u>, <u>CREST syndrome</u>, <u>Sjogren syndrome</u>)<br><br>* <u>Inflammatory myopathies</u> (e.g., <u>polymyositis</u>, <u>dermatomyositis</u>, <u>inclusion body myositis</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Mucosal</u> disorders<br><br>* Local infection (e.g., <u>epiglottitis</u>, <u>acute tonsillitis</u>)<br><br>* Corrosive injury (e.g., thermal or chemical burn)<br><br>* <u>Zenker diverticulum</u><br><br>* <u>Mucositis</u> (e.g., caused by <u>radiation therapy</u> or <u>chemotherapy</u>)<br><br>* <u>Oropharyngeal cancer</u><br><br>* Head and <u>neck dissection</u><br><br>* Extramural disorders<br><br>* <u>Deep neck infection</u><br><br>* Cricopharyngeal muscle spasm<br><br>* <u>Osteophytes</u><br><br>* <u>Thyroglossal duct cyst</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Esophageal dysphagia</u> | <br><br>* <u>Achalasia</u>  [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[6]](/library/8bbOvH)<br><br>* <u>GERD</u><br><br>* <u>Esophageal hypermotility disorders</u><br><br>* <u>Mixed connective tissue diseases</u>  [[6]](/library/8bbOvH)[[7]](/library/2CbTrD)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Intraluminal disorders: impacted foreign object or food bolus<br><br>* <u>Mucosal</u> disorders (intrinsic narrowing)<br><br>* <u>Esophagitis</u> (e.g., <u>infectious esophagitis</u>, <u>eosinophilic esophagitis</u>, <u>corrosive esophagitis</u>, or secondary to <u>GERD</u>, <u>chemotherapy</u>, or <u>radiotherapy</u>)<br><br>* Esophageal webs (e.g., in <u>Plummer-Vinson syndrome</u>)<br><br>* <u>Esophageal rings</u> (e.g., <u>Schatzki ring</u>)<br><br>* <u>Esophageal cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Esophageal diverticulum</u><br><br>* Autoimmune conditions (e.g., <u>CREST syndrome</u>, <u>Crohn disease</u>, <u>Behcet disease</u>, <u>pemphigus syndromes</u>)<br><br>* Extrinsic compression<br><br>* <u>Thyromegaly</u>, substernal <u>thyroid</u><br><br>* Hilar <u>lymphadenopathy</u>,<br><br>* <u>Neoplasia</u> (e.g., <u>mediastinal</u> <u>tumor</u>, <u>thyroid</u> <u>tumor</u>)<br><br>* Cardiac dysphagia: a group of cardiovascular anomalies that cause dysphagia due to compression of the <u>esophagus</u><br><br>* Includes <u>vascular ring</u> anomalies (e.g., <u>double aortic arch</u>), dysphagia lusoria (abnormal <u>right subclavian artery</u>), severe <u>atherosclerosis</u>, and <u>aneurysms</u><br><br>* Dysphagia megalatriensis: compression of the <u>esophagus</u> by a giant <u>left atrium</u>, most commonly caused by <u>mitral stenosis</u> due to <u>rheumatic heart disease</u> and a left <u>atrial myxoma</u><br><br>* <u>Hiatal hernia</u><br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Dysphagia should be distinguished from <u>xerostomia</u>, <u>globus pharyngeus</u>, and <u>presbyphagia</u>. [[8]](/library/SCbyrD)




> [!WARNING]
> Do not assume a diagnosis of <u>presbyphagia</u> in elderly patients with difficulty <u>swallowing</u>. Dysphagia is an <u>alarm symptom</u> and should be investigated thoroughly to determine its underlying etiology and start appropriate treatment.

---

## Approach

A detailed clinical history and <u>physical examination</u> in patients with dysphagia can help categorize symptoms and select the best initial diagnostic test.




### Clinical evaluation [[6]](/library/8bbOvH)[[7]](/library/2CbTrD)[[9]](/library/s5ctl10)




* <u>Characterize dysphagia</u>.

* Distinguish between esophageal and <u>oropharyngeal dysphagia</u>.

* Distinguish between <u>motility-related dysphagia</u> and <u>structural dysphagia</u>

* Observe a swallow.

* <u>Coughing</u> on <u>swallowing</u> indicates a high <u>aspiration</u> risk.

* <u>Nasopharyngeal</u> <u>regurgitation</u> is suggestive of <u>oropharyngeal dysphagia</u>.

* Identify <u>red flags for dysphagia</u>.

* Perform a complete <u>physical examination</u>, with particular importance to

* Neurological evaluation (including <u>cranial nerve examination</u>)

* Absent <u>gag reflex</u> and facial asymmetry indicate <u>cranial nerve palsies</u> (e.g., due to <u>stroke</u>).

* <u>Ptosis</u>, <u>diplopia</u>, deviation of the <u>tongue</u> should increase the suspicion for <u>ALS</u>.

* <u>Head and neck examination</u>: for <u>lymphadenopathy</u>, <u>thyromegaly</u>

* Identify the likely etiology based on history and examination.

* Select the appropriate initial diagnostic test based on the likely site and location of dysphagia.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Oropharyngeal dysphagia</u> should be identified promptly, as it increases the risk of <u>aspiration</u>. <u>Oropharyngeal dysphagia</u> and <u>esophageal dysphagia</u> may occur simultaneously. [[7]](/library/2CbTrD)




> [!WARNING]
> Acute dysphagia can be caused by food impaction or a <u>stroke</u> and requires prompt evaluation.




### Characterization of dysphagia




| <br>Clinical characterization of dysphagia [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[6]](/library/8bbOvH)[[10]](/library/zsbrxE)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Description of dysphagia | Possible associated findings and conditions |
| <u>Oropharyngeal dysphagia</u> | <br><br>* Difficulty initiating <u>swallowing</u>, which can lead to repeat swallow attempts<br><br>* Predominantly experienced in the throat or neck<br><br>* May be associated with <u>coughing</u> or a choking sensation early in the <u>swallowing</u> process.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Reduced <u>cough reflex</u><br><br>* Drooling<br><br>* Nasal <u>regurgitation</u><br><br>* Voice changes (nasal speech, wet voice)<br><br>* Recurrent <u>pneumonia</u> (<u>aspiration pneumonia</u>)<br><br>* <u>Malnutrition</u> and/or <u>anorexia</u><br><br>* Neurological symptoms (e.g., <u>dysarthria</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Esophageal dysphagia</u> | <br><br>* Symptoms occur seconds after <u>swallowing</u><br><br>* Predominantly experienced retrosternally<br><br>* May be associated with <u>coughing</u> late in the <u>swallowing</u> process<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Halitosis</u><br><br>* Bolus impaction<br><br><br> |
| <u>Motility-related dysphagia</u> | <br><br>* Dysphagia predominantly with liquids (or liquids and solid food)<br><br>* May be aggravated by cold foods<br><br>* Intermittent symptoms or progression of symptoms over a long duration (months to years) [[6]](/library/8bbOvH)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Esophageal hypermotility disorders</u>: episodic central <u>chest pain</u>.<br><br>* <u>Esophageal hypomotility</u> disorders<br><br>* <u>Regurgitation</u> of undigested food (<u>achalasia</u>)<br><br>* Systemic features of underlying disease (e.g., <u>scleroderma</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Structural dysphagia</u> | <br><br>* Dysphagia predominantly with solid food (or initially to solids that progressed to liquids)<br><br>* May be aggravated by large food boli and dense food<br><br><br> | <br>* Depends on the underlying cause; examples include:<br><br>* <u>Symptoms of GERD</u> in <u>reflux esophagitis</u><br><br>* <u>Red flags for dysphagia</u> in <u>esophageal cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Fever</u> in infectious causes (e.g., <u>deep neck infection</u>, <u>infectious esophagitis</u>)<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Dysphagia predominantly with solid food should raise suspicion for an underlying structural disorder, including <u>malignancy</u>. Dysphagia predominantly with liquids is suggestive of an <u>esophageal motility disorder</u>. [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)




### Red flags for dysphagia [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[7]](/library/2CbTrD)[[9]](/library/s5ctl10)




Dysphagia is an <u>alarm feature</u> itself and should be evaluated thoroughly. However, the following features should raise suspicion for <u>malignancy</u> as the underlying etiology.




* > 50 years of age at onset

* <u>Clinically significant involuntary weight loss</u>

* Symptom progression over a short period of time (e.g., < 4 months)  [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)

* Evidence of <u>GI bleeding</u>

* Recurrent <u>vomiting</u>

* History of cancer





> [!TIP]
> Elderly patients with recent <u>pneumonia</u> should be screened for dysphagia. [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)




### Initial diagnostics [[6]](/library/8bbOvH)[[9]](/library/s5ctl10)




See dedicated sections below for details.




* <u>Oropharyngeal dysphagia</u>: <u>modified barium swallow</u>

* <u>Esophageal dysphagia</u>

* Patients ≥ 50 years of age, and patients < 50 years of age with any <u>red flag for dysphagia</u>: <u>EGD</u>

* Patients < 50 years of age with no <u>red flags for dysphagia</u>: Consider a 4-week trial of <u>acid suppression therapy</u> before <u>EGD</u>.

* Consider <u>neuroimaging</u>  and supplementary <u>laboratory studies</u>  as needed, guided by the <u>pretest probability</u> of the underlying etiology.

## Oropharyngeal dysphagia

### Etiology




| <br>Common etiologies of oropharyngeal dysphagia [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[8]](/library/SCbyrD)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Characteristic clinical features | Diagnostics |
| Neuromuscular disorders | <br><u>CNS</u> disorders <br> | <br><br>* Dysphagia predominantly with liquids<br><br>* Onset depends on the specific etiology<br><br>* Acute: suggestive of a <u>stroke</u><br><br>* Insidious: suggestive of <u>neurodegenerative disorders</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Modified barium swallow</u><br><br>* Difficulty in the initial phases of the <u>swallowing</u> process<br><br>* Evidence of <u>aspiration</u> may be seen<br><br>* <u>Neuroimaging</u> (e.g., <u>cMRI</u>): Findings depend on the specific etiology.<br><br>* See “<u>Neuroimaging for ischemic stroke</u>.”<br><br>* For findings in specific <u>neurodegenerative diseases</u>, see the relevant articles, e.g., <u>Parkinson disease</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u>, <u>progressive supranuclear palsy</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <br>Muscular disorders<br> [[11]](/library/CTcqGb0)[[12]](/library/xTcEGb0)<br> | <br><br>* Dysphagia predominantly with liquids<br><br>* Subacute onset<br><br>* Usually associated with systemic features of progressive <u>weakness</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>FEES</u> and manometry<br><br>* Weak pharyngeal muscle contraction<br><br>* Ineffective swallow<br><br>* Pharyngeal food residue<br><br>* <u>Velopharyngeal insufficiency</u> may be present<br><br> |  |
| Obstructive and structural causes | <br>External compression<br> [[13]](/library/YWcnPY0)<br> | <br><br>* Visible or palpable masses in the neck or <u>oropharynx</u> may be present<br><br>* Additional features depend on the specific etiology.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Esophageal barium swallow</u>: <u>mass effect</u><br><br>* Imaging to identify the etiology; e.g.,<br><br>* <u>X-ray</u> neck for cervical <u>osteophytes</u><br><br>* CT or <u>MRI</u> <u>oropharynx</u> and neck to assess masses and the degree of compression<br><br>* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: provides supportive evidence of underlying etiology<br><br><br> |
| <br>Head and neck malignancies [[14]](/library/ETc8sb0)<br> | <br>* Progressive features that vary depending on the location<br><br>* <u>Oral cavity</u>: nonhealing ulceroproliferative mass<br><br>* <u>Oropharynx</u>: <u>sore throat</u>, chronic dysphagia, and persistent <u>odynophagia</u><br><br>* <u>Larynx</u>: <u>hoarseness</u> of voice<br><br>* <u>Hypopharynx</u>: cervical <u>adenopathy</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Endoscopy (e.g., <u>nasopharyngeal laryngoscopy</u>): visualization of the <u>tumor</u><br><br>* Imaging (e.g., CT, <u>MRI</u>, or PET) of the head and neck: localize the site of oropharyngeal compression; assess the extent of the <u>tumor</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Secondary to treatment, interventions, or injury [[15]](/library/vTcAsb0)[[16]](/library/DTc1Gb0)<br> | <br><br>* Prior therapy for head and neck malignancies<br><br>* Resection of tumors<br><br>* <u>Neck dissection</u><br><br>* <u>Radiotherapy</u><br><br>* History of other surgical interventions in the neck<br><br>* Corrosive injury of the <u>oropharynx</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Usually a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on history<br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Zenker diverticulum</u> [[4]](/library/t1bXis)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Halitosis</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Modified barium swallow</u>: contrast-filled pouch protruding from the <u>pharynx</u> [[13]](/library/YWcnPY0)<br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Oropharyngeal dysphagia</u> is commonly caused by neuromuscular and systemic conditions.




### Clinical swallow evaluation [[17]](/library/VqdGxI0)




* Description: a clinical assessment of the anatomy, function, and reflexes of the mouth, <u>tongue</u>, and <u>mandible</u> along with a trial of food and liquid

* Indications: neurological conditions with associated dysphagia (e.g., <u>ALS</u>, <u>Parkinson disease</u>, acute <u>stroke</u>, <u>Guillain-Barré syndrome</u>)

* Goal: to guide decisions on dietary modification (e.g., pureed food, thickened liquids, <u>nasogastric tube</u>, <u>percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy</u>) and further testing for <u>oropharyngeal dysphagia</u>

* Interpretation

* Positive test: patient is unable to drink continuously, coughs up after the <u>swallowing</u> attempt, and/or has a wet, gargling, or hoarse voice

* A <u>confirmatory test</u> (e.g., <u>modified barium swallow</u>) should be performed if <u>clinical swallow evaluation</u> is positive.





### Diagnostics [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[7]](/library/2CbTrD)[[9]](/library/s5ctl10)




A multidisciplinary evaluation involving speech-language pathologists, neurologists, and otolaryngologists is recommended for a comprehensive evaluation.




* <u>Modified barium swallow</u>  [[6]](/library/8bbOvH)[[10]](/library/zsbrxE)

* Preferred test for suspected <u>oropharyngeal dysphagia</u> [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)

* Provides functional evaluation of <u>swallowing</u> and can be used to assess the risk of <u>aspiration</u>

* Endoscopic evaluation of the <u>nasopharynx</u>

* Structural assessment: <u>nasopharyngeal laryngoscopy</u>

* Functional assessment: <u>fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing</u> (<u>FEES</u>)

* Supplementary modality to <u>modified barium swallow</u> [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)

* Direct assessment of the oropharyngeal phase of <u>swallowing</u>

* Superior evaluation of <u>structural dysphagia</u> compared with <u>barium swallow</u> [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)

* Pharyngoesophageal <u>high-resolution manometry</u> : Can help identify patients who are likely to benefit from a myotomy [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)





> [!TIP]
> Consider <u>EGD</u> to rule out an esophageal etiology for dysphagia in patients in whom an oropharyngeal etiology has been ruled out. [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)




### Treatment [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)[[18]](/library/LCbwsD)[[19]](/library/MCbMsD)




Management is primarily supportive and should be tailored to each patient, focus on symptom control, minimize <u>aspiration</u> risk, and ensure adequate nutrition. <u>Goals of care</u> should be discussed before considering interventional therapy (including <u>enteral feeding</u>) for dysphagia in elderly patients.




* <u>Swallowing</u> <u>rehabilitation</u>: compensatory strategies aimed to direct the bolus towards the <u>esophagus</u> and minimize <u>aspiration</u> risk [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)[[18]](/library/LCbwsD)

* Postural techniques (e.g., eating upright, chin tuck , head turn )

* Exercises and retraining of the <u>tongue</u>, <u>jaw</u>, and neck

* Optimization of nutrition

* Diet modification as needed (e.g., thickening of liquids, pureeing solid food, small morsels).

* Consider temporary <u>nasogastric tube</u> feeding (e.g., in patients with acute <u>stroke</u>).  [[20]](/library/mMcV610)

* See “<u>Specialized nutrition support</u>” for details.

* Management of the underlying cause, e.g.: 

* Optimize pharmacotherapy of underlying <u>neurodegenerative conditions</u> (e.g., <u>Parkinson disease</u>).

* Surgical intervention for <u>Zenker diverticulum</u>

* <u>Aspiration</u> prevention <u>surgery</u> [[21]](/library/hScczb0)

* Consider in patients at a high risk of <u>aspiration</u> despite other supportive measures.

* Examples include <u>percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy</u>, tracheotomy, and endolaryngeal <u>stenting</u>

## Esophageal dysphagia

### Etiology




| <br>Common etiologies of esophageal dysphagia [[6]](/library/8bbOvH)[[9]](/library/s5ctl10)<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | Characteristic clinical features | Diagnostics | Management |
| <br><u>Esophagitis</u><br>(most common cause of dysphagia) [[6]](/library/8bbOvH)[[9]](/library/s5ctl10)[[13]](/library/YWcnPY0)<br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Reflux esophagitis</u> (<u>GERD</u>)  [[22]](/library/qO0CtT)[[23]](/library/SMcyL10)<br>* Typically associated with <u>heartburn</u> and <u>regurgitation</u><br><br>* <u>Eosinophilic esophagitis</u><br><br>* Intermittent dysphagia<br><br>* Possible history of <u>food bolus impaction</u><br><br>* Associated with <u>atopic</u> features and/or history of <u>asthma</u> or <u>allergies</u><br><br>* <u>Infectious esophagitis</u> [[24]](/library/D2c1Pb0)<br><br>* More common in <u>immunosuppressed</u> individuals<br><br>* Typically associated with <u>odynophagia</u><br><br>* Systemic signs of infection may be present<br><br>* <u>Pill esophagitis</u>: recent history of medication use<br><br>* Radiation <u>esophagitis</u>: recent history of <u>radiotherapy</u> to the central chest<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>EGD</u><br><br>* Common: <u>erythema</u>, <u>edema</u>, <u>friability</u>, <u>erosions</u><br><br>* Specific changes: e.g., <u>ulcers</u>, <u>plaques</u>, <u>thrush</u>, depending on the specific etiology<br><br>* <u>Histopathology</u>: inflammatory changes and infiltrates, depending on the specific etiology<br><br>* See “<u>EGD</u>” and “Pathology” in “<u>Approach to esophagitis</u>” for details.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Depends on the underlying cause<br><br>* See “<u>GERD</u>” and “<u>Esophagitis</u>” for details.<br><br><br> |
| <br>Functional esophageal disorders (e.g., <u>nonerosive reflux disease</u>, reflux hypersensitivity)  [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)<br> |  | <br>* Dysphagia that may be associated with retrosternal <u>chest pain</u> and/or <u>heartburn</u><br><br> | <br>* A diagnosis of exclusion<br><br> | <br><br>* Reassurance<br><br>* Recommend avoidance of triggers.<br><br>* Consider a trial of <u>PPIs</u> and <u>tricyclic antidepressants</u>.  [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)<br><br><br> |
| Structural and obstructive disorders | <br><u>Esophageal cancer</u> [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[25]](/library/pk0LKT)<br> | <br><br>* Dysphagia predominantly with solid food<br><br>* <u>Risk factors for esophageal cancer</u> and/or <u>red flags for dysphagia</u> may be present.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>EGD</u>: ulceroproliferative mass <u>friable</u> mass<br><br>* <u>Esophageal barium swallow</u>: <u>apple core lesion</u><br><br>* <u>Histopathology</u>: <u>adenocarcinoma</u> or <u>squamous cell carcinoma</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Curative or <u>palliative treatment</u> based on the <u>TNM stage</u> of <u>esophageal cancer</u><br><br> |

> [!TIP]
> <u>Opioid</u> use can cause <u>esophageal hypomotility</u> and thereby dysphagia (<u>opioid</u>-induced esophageal dysfunction). [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)




### Diagnostics [[6]](/library/8bbOvH)[[7]](/library/2CbTrD)[[9]](/library/s5ctl10)




Consult a gastroenterologist early for a comprehensive evaluation. [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)




* <u>Esophagogastroduodenoscopy</u> (<u>EGD</u>): preferred initial test for most patients [[7]](/library/2CbTrD)[[9]](/library/s5ctl10)

* Allows for direct visualization of <u>mucosal</u> lesions and structural abnormalities

* <u>Biopsies</u> can be taken during the procedure.

* Simultaneous therapeutic intervention (e.g., dilation) or <u>endoscopic ultrasound</u> is possible

* <u>Esophageal barium swallow</u> [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[7]](/library/2CbTrD)

* Consider as an initial test in the following cases:

* High likelihood of <u>esophageal stricture</u> (e.g., history of <u>esophageal caustic injury</u>, <u>surgery</u>, or radiation)  [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[32]](/library/55cik10)

* If <u>EGD</u> is not immediately available

* Suspected <u>achalasia</u> if manometry is not immediately available

* Second-line test (adjunct) if initial <u>EGD</u> is normal [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)

* <u>High-resolution esophageal manometry</u> 

* <u>Gold standard</u> for diagnosing <u>esophageal motility disorders</u>

* Suspected <u>esophageal motility disorder</u> in individuals with a normal <u>EGD</u> and <u>barium swallow</u>.  [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[7]](/library/2CbTrD)[[33]](/library/mCbVsD)

* Thoracic imaging: if extrinsic esophageal compression is suspected (e.g., due to <u>goiter</u>, <u>thoracic aortic aneurysm</u>, <u>mediastinal mass</u>)





### Treatment [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[9]](/library/s5ctl10)[[19]](/library/MCbMsD)




Depends on the underlying cause. See “<u>Overview of esophageal dysphagia</u>” and dedicated articles for details; examples include:




* Pharmacotherapy: e.g.,

* <u>PPI</u> for <u>reflux esophagitis</u>

* <u>Smooth muscle</u> relaxants for <u>esophageal motility disorders</u>

* <u>Swallowed aerosolized steroids</u> for <u>eosinophilic esophagitis</u>

* Endoscopic intervention

* <u>Botox</u> injections: to control hypertonia

* Dilation: for etiologies that cause significant narrowing (e.g., <u>achalasia</u>, <u>esophageal rings</u> or webs, strictures)

* <u>Diverticulotomy</u>: for <u>esophageal diverticula</u>

* <u>Surgery</u>

* Myotomy: Consider for refractory <u>esophageal hypermotility disorders</u>.

* Curative or palliative <u>tumor</u> resection (e.g., in <u>pharyngeal cancer</u> or <u>esophageal cancer</u>)

* Surgical resection of refractory rings and/or strictures

* Supportive therapy: Optimize nutrition of patients with dysphagia refractory to therapy.

* Diet modification as needed (e.g., pureeing solid food, taking small bites, chewing carefully).

* Consider temporary <u>nasogastric tube</u> feeding (e.g., in patients with acute <u>stroke</u>).  [[20]](/library/mMcV610)

* See “<u>Specialized nutrition support</u>” for details.





> [!TIP]
> In older patients, <u>discuss goals of care</u> before considering interventional therapy. [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)




> [!TIP]
> In patients < 50 years of age with characteristic features of <u>GERD</u> and no <u>alarm features</u> for <u>malignancy</u>, a trial of empiric treatment with <u>PPIs</u> for 4 weeks may be considered. Persistent dysphagia despite empiric treatment necessitates evaluation by <u>EGD</u>. [[3]](/library/3NaSaO)[[9]](/library/s5ctl10)




> [!WARNING]
> In all patients with unexplained solid food dysphagia, <u>biopsies</u> should be obtained from normal-appearing <u>mucosa</u> of the mid-third and <u>distal</u> <u>esophagus</u> to evaluate for <u>eosinophilic esophagitis</u>. [[9]](/library/s5ctl10)

---

## Complications

* Esophageal bolus impaction: usually manifests as acute dysphagia

* <u>Aspiration pneumonia</u>: common complication of <u>oropharyngeal dysphagia</u> [[7]](/library/2CbTrD)

* <u>Malnutrition</u> (see “<u>Specialized nutrition support</u>” for management)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
